summary:
On a mission to Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 44 minutes to get an answer, so the crew has to look after their own health. NOVA is a medical system that runs on the spacecraft, on NASA's F Prime flight software, and does not need Earth to work.

Each morning a medical station identifies the astronaut and takes a one-minute check. The data goes into a 3D digital twin of each crew member, which forecasts every vital sign and warns before it crosses the limit set by the flight surgeon. A daily check-in on each astronaut's phone tracks mood, sleep and energy. When there is a medical emergency, NOVA alerts the crew and guides them step by step with augmented reality over the patient's body, including in zero gravity. It also keeps track of the mission's radiation dose and sends the crew to the shelter during a solar storm. Every night it sends a report to Earth and receives signed updates.
details:
THE PROBLEM

NASA's Human Research Program identifies five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment. On the way to Mars the round-trip delay to Earth can reach 44 minutes, and during solar conjunction there is no link for about two weeks. The crew needs to assess and act on their health without waiting for the ground.

WHAT NOVA DOES

Daily check. A station we built identifies each astronaut with an NFC card and records an ECG with an AD8232 board on an Arduino. It is designed to add oxygen, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, cognitive fatigue and gut microbiota.

Digital twin. Each crew member has a 3D anatomical model where every organ can be selected to see its function and current status, colored by their vital signs. NOVA forecasts the trend of each signal and warns before it reaches the flight-surgeon limit. It tracks 18 signals per person, including the ones named in the challenge: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood.

Mental health. A one-minute daily check-in on each phone records mood, sleep and energy. NOVA shows it as a constellation for each person and for the whole crew, so a crewmate who is struggling is noticed early. Women's health is included and private by default.

Emergencies. NOVA has 13 medical protocols, and each step cites its source and page. It alerts the ship PC, the station and every phone at the same time. During an emergency it reads fixed protocol text; the language model is never used to decide what to do.

Augmented reality. Using a camera, NOVA fits the anatomy onto the patient's body, tracks the rescuer's hands and corrects their movements in real time. CPR technique changes with gravity, following the published guidelines for zero g and for Mars. We tested it at the hackathon on our own team. In the future we want it to guide complex procedures, including surgery.

Radiation. NOVA estimates the mission dose using the rates measured by Curiosity's MSL RAD instrument and compares it with NASA's 600 mSv career limit. During a solar particle event every screen raises an alert and NOVA guides the crew to the shelter.

Link with Earth. Every night F Prime sends a report to Earth as CCSDS packets. Updates come back signed with ed25519, and the ship checks the signature before installing them, with automatic rollback if something fails. The next step is knowledge distillation: a larger teacher model on Earth trains the smaller model that runs on board.

HOW IT IS BUILT

The ship PC runs Tauri and Rust, NOVA Station is a tablet connected to an Arduino, and each astronaut has a React Native app. All of them talk to the same F Prime core written in C++. Everything runs locally: llama.cpp with Qwen3-4B, whisper.cpp for speech, Kokoro for the voice and MediaPipe for body and hand tracking. A library of 41 open medical sources, split into 35,830 passages, lets NOVA show the exact page behind each answer.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Astronauts are not medical doctors, so every screen uses plain language and color-coded status. The system must keep working with no link to Earth, so nothing depends on the cloud. Safety comes first: emergency guidance is fixed and sourced, and any update from Earth must be signed before it is installed.

-

The narration in the project video on our website is an AI-generated voice (Google Gemini). An AI coding assistant helped us write and debug parts of the code, and we reviewed and tested all of it. No NASA logos or branding were generated or modified with AI. The music is "Unbreakable Spirit" by RaspberryMusic (Pixabay license).
